title: Dead thief's accomplice speaks out: Man challenges SIU ruling that death was `unavoidable'
article: Police officers in an unmarked van chasing a petty theft suspect fleeing on a bicycle almost sideswiped him before he was knocked to the asphalt and his head crushed under the wheel of the van, according to the suspect's alleged partner in crime.

Speaking out for the first time since the June 22 pursuit in the Byward Market, Eric Albert, 30, challenged Wednesday's ruling by the province's police watchdog that the death of his friend, 38-year- old Benoit Aube, was an accident.

"There was no reason for him to die just for attempted theft," Mr. Albert said. "The cops rampaged him and for what? Attempted theft in a car, not to steal a car, but to look for loose change. We were on bikes. How fast could we possibly move?"

Mr. Aube was riding his bike east on one-way Clarence Street shortly after 1 a.m. on June 22 when an undercover van carrying two members of the Ottawa police tactical squad hit the cyclist and then stopped with the wheel resting on his head, near Cumberland Street. The call came in as a "theft in progress" involving two suspects.

Mr. Albert, an admitted "petty criminal," was arrested without incident a short distance away, on York Street. He is to appear in court July 25, charged with two counts of attempted accessory to an offence, possession of break-and-enter instruments and failing to comply with a probation order.

Witnesses said Mr. Aube lay under the van, bleeding heavily, for more than 30 minutes before firefighters jacked it up to free him. He was taken to hospital, clinging to life. With a fracture at the base of his skull, Mr. Aube died at the Ottawa Hospital's General campus the next day.
Their last day together was a good one, Mr. Albert said. "We partied all day. It was a beautiful day. Here and there, parties, a couple beers, all day long."
When midnight came, the men found themselves drunk and "doing stupid things" near the Beer Store on Bruyere Street, Mr. Albert said.

"We checked to see if a car's doors were locked. We wanted to look for loose change. We were trying to open the car's doors and then we went downtown. They noticed us doing stupid things and then they followed us."
Acknowledging "I was pretty drunk and I forget some spots," Mr. Albert remembers the pursuit starting somewhere near Clarence Street.
"They had been following us. Why wouldn't they call in another three or four cruisers and block the street off?"
Mr. Albert said he spent 15 hours in a cell before members of the Special Investigations Unit came to interview him.
After a month-long investigation, the SIU cleared the officer who was driving the van, ruling the collision that killed Mr. Aube was "unavoidable."

The SIU, a civilian agency that investigates circumstances involving police and civilians that result in serious injury or death, concluded there are no grounds to believe the officer committed a criminal offence during the chase. The agency said the pursuit started on Murray Street, where the officer was driving parallel to Mr. Aube. The pursuit continued to Clarence Street, the SIU said, where Mr. Aube turned in front of the van and was run over.
SIU director Peter Tinsley said the van was moving slowly and "the collision was unavoidable as a result of the unexpected movement of Mr. Aube's bicycle into the path of the police vehicle."
The SIU spoke with the officer, interviewed 10 civilian and police witnesses, and analyzed forensic evidence.
"There is something wrong with the decision," Mr. Albert said. "It freaks me right out."

Mr. Albert said Mr. Aube had to ride his bike slowly because he had broken discs in his back due to a weightlifting accident in prison. Always on his bicycle, he was a familiar figure among the city's homeless since his release from prison in April.

"He could hardly walk, that's why he was riding his bike all the time," Mr. Albert said. The men were living at the Mission on Waller Street. Mr. Aube didn't want to go back to prison -- so he took off, Mr. Albert said.
